evidence.claim: A gravel loop follows older journeys across the Continental Divide.
evidence.quote: The Byway is a single-lane gravel road with pullouts.

evidence.claim: A gravel loop follows older journeys across the Continental Divide.
evidence.quote: They followed long-established Indian trails.

evidence.claim: The Lewis and Clark Back Country Byway makes a 36-mile loop from Tendoy through river valley, sagebrush grasslands, mountain forests and high desert canyons.
evidence.quote: The Byway traverses four habitats: river valley, sagebrush grasslands, mountain forests and meadows, and high desert canyons.

evidence.claim: This single-lane gravel road has pullouts, steep exposed slopes without guardrails and grades approaching 20 percent.
evidence.quote: The Byway is a single-lane gravel road with pullouts.

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management presents it as a journey through scenery and history on the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail and Continental Divide National Scenic Trail.
evidence.quote: The Lewis and Clark Back Country Byway and Adventure Road is a 36 mile loop drive through a beautiful and historic landscape on the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail and the Continental Divide National Scenic Trail.

evidence.claim: a 36-mile loop from Tendoy
evidence.quote: The Lewis and Clark Back Country Byway AND ADVENTURE ROAD Tendoy, Idaho The Lewis and Clark Back Country Byway and Adventure Road is a 36 mile loop drive

evidence.claim: steep exposed slopes without guardrails
evidence.quote: Parts of the Byway traverse steep, exposed slopes and there are no guardrails.

evidence.claim: grades approaching 20 percent
evidence.quote: expect some steep grades, at times approaching 20%.

evidence.claim: The expedition followed established trails in the homeland of the Agai Dika Shoshone, later known as the Lemhi Shoshone.
evidence.quote: They followed long-established Indian trails. This is the homeland of the Agai Dika [“salmon eater”] Shoshone, who came to be known as the Lemhi Shoshone

evidence.claim: After the railroad reached Dillon in 1880, Salmon residents pooled resources to build a road over the pass to Red Rock’s rail station.
evidence.quote: When the Utah & Northern railroad reached Dillon, Montana, in 1880, the citizens of Salmon pooled their resources to build a road over the pass to the Red Rock rail station south of Dillon.

evidence.claim: Stage service began in the late 1880s and lasted until the railway reached Salmon over Bannock Pass in 1910.
evidence.quote: it became the Red Rock-Salmon City Stage Road when stagecoach service began in the late1880s.

evidence.claim: lasted until the railway reached Salmon over Bannock Pass in 1910
evidence.quote: until 1910, when the Gilmore and Pittsburgh RR was completed over Bannock Pass to Salmon.

evidence.claim: Drive clockwise from Tendoy along the Lemhi back road, then climb Warm Springs Wood Road into the Beaverhead Mountains.
evidence.quote: First is the “Lemhi back road” in the Lemhi Valley near Tendoy. Second is the “Warm Springs Wood Road” [185] from the valley into the Beaverhead Mountains to Lemhi Pass.

evidence.claim: Past the Flag Unfurling Monument and Pattee Creek Overlook, the road turns south near the Continental Divide toward Lemhi Pass.
evidence.quote: At the beautiful meadows that are the headwaters of Pattee Creek, the road turns south to contour near the Continental Divide for several miles.

evidence.claim: Agency Creek Road returns to Tendoy, passing Horseshoe Bend Creek below the pass.
evidence.quote: The third segment is the Agency Creek road [013] from Lemhi Pass back to Tendoy.

evidence.claim: Past the Flag Unfurling Monument and Pattee Creek Overlook
evidence.quote: Mile 8.2—The Flag Unfurling Monument

evidence.claim: Past the Flag Unfurling Monument and Pattee Creek Overlook
evidence.quote: Mile 9.6—Pattee Creek Overlook

evidence.claim: passing Horseshoe Bend Creek below the pass
evidence.quote: Mile 25.0—Horseshoe Bend Creek

evidence.claim: The monument marks Lewis’s advance party displaying the United States flag on August 13, 1805, the first such display in present-day Idaho.
evidence.quote: The Flag Unfurling Monument commemorates the display of the U. S. flag by Lewis’s advance party on August 13th, 1805.

evidence.claim: Earlier contact that day began when the four explorers encountered three Shoshone women.
evidence.quote: Captain Lewis’s advance party first made contact with the Lemhi Shoshone on August 13, 1805, when they suddenly came upon three Shoshone women.

evidence.claim: Lewis gave them gifts and persuaded them to lead his party toward their encampment.
evidence.quote: After “pacifying” them with gifts, Lewis persuaded the women to take the 12 explorers to their encampment to speak with the chief.

evidence.claim: On the way, they met Chief Cameahwait and sixty warriors.
evidence.quote: On the way there they met the chief and sixty of his warriors

evidence.claim: When the women showed Cameahwait the gifts, he welcomed the strangers as friends.
evidence.quote: When the women showed Chief Cameahwait the gifts Lewis had given them, he welcomed the four strangers as friends.

evidence.claim: the first such display in present-day Idaho
evidence.quote: This was the first time the Stars and Stripes were unfurled in present-day Idaho.

evidence.claim: The Shoshones called this crossing We-yah-vee and used it for generations before Lewis and Clark arrived.
evidence.quote: The Shoshones called the pass We-yah-vee. They and other tribes had used it for many generations before the Corps of Discovery arrived in 1805.

evidence.claim: On August 12, 1805, Lewis reached the divide and recorded more mountain ranges to the west, their tops partly covered in snow.
evidence.quote: I discovered immence ranges of mountains still to the west of with their tops still partially covered with snow*.

evidence.claim: Later travelers crossed by stagecoach: eight dollars bought a one-way, twelve-hour trip from Salmon to Red Rock.
evidence.quote: $8.00 bought a one-way ticket for the twelve hour trip from Salmon to Red Rock.

evidence.claim: The pass itself owes its low saddle to a fault zone, where fractured rock erodes faster than the surrounding rock.
evidence.quote: Lemhi Pass exists because it straddles a fault zone characterized by broken and fractured rock that erodes more rapidly than the surrounding rock, creating the low “saddle”

evidence.claim: On August 12, 1805, Lewis reached the divide
evidence.quote: On August 12, 1805 Meriwether Lewis and three other members of the Lewis and Clark Expedition crossed the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass.

evidence.claim: Lewis and his men drank where Horseshoe Bend Creek joins Agency Creek, 0.4 mile below the sharp road curve.
evidence.quote: Lewis and his men drank from this creek where it joins Agency Creek 0.4 mile below this sharp curve.

evidence.claim: After seeing the mountains beyond Lemhi Pass, they took comfort in believing this water would eventually reach the Columbia River.
evidence.quote: They consoled themselves following their shocking view from Lemhi Pass with the belief that they were drinking from a stream that would eventually reach the Columbia River.

evidence.claim: Agency Creek rises west of Lemhi Pass and flows to the Lemhi River at Tendoy.
evidence.quote: Agency Creek rises on the west side of Lemhi Pass and then flows westerly to join the Lemhi River at Tendoy, Idaho.

evidence.claim: Allow at least three hours.
evidence.quote: Plan on taking a minimum of three hours to drive the Byway.

evidence.claim: Agency Creek Road is not suitable for trailers, buses or motorhomes.
evidence.quote: It is not appropriate for trailers, buses, or motorhomes.

evidence.claim: The byway is normally snow-free from early June through October.
evidence.quote: The Byway is normally free of snow from early June through October.

evidence.claim: The loop gains and loses 4,000 feet in elevation, and the agency guide calls for at least three hours to drive it.
evidence.quote: With a 4,000 foot gain and loss in elevation

evidence.claim: the agency guide calls for at least three hours to drive it.
evidence.quote: Plan on taking a minimum of three hours to drive the Byway.

evidence.claim: Lewis had set out to find the Shoshone because he hoped their horses could carry the expedition’s baggage over the divide.
evidence.quote: Lewis set out on foot with a small party to find the Shoshone, Sacagawea’s people, whose horses he hoped would help portage the Expedition’s baggage over the divide.

evidence.claim: Stations supplied meals and replacement horses and mules; the stage company operated as many as fourteen coaches and twelve freight wagons.
evidence.quote: Stations along the way provided meals and fresh mules and horses. The stage company employed from 35-40 people and operated up to fourteen coaches and a dozen freight wagons.

flags: Road advice comes from the cached 2016 agency guide; the requested checked date records this cache review, not live road-condition verification.
The cache does not supply the byway designation date.
Horseshoe Bend Creek is shorter than 90 words because the stop-specific evidence is thin.
The flag-site article describes two women; the agency guide describes three. The story follows the agency guide and separates the monument from the encounter location.
Moment order follows the agency guide’s clockwise mileage; material’s Lemhi Pass mile reflects the opposite approach.
Sacagawea/Sacajawea and Shoshone/Shoshoni spellings vary among cached sources; unused biographical material was omitted.
